# Antiquity · c. 200 CE

Around 200 CE: Silk Road, Americas exchange, African networks. Drag the timeline to move through time; click a dot to read that story here.

## silk-road
### Rome, India and Han China
spot: 39.65, 66.97
view: fit
site: Rome · 41.9, 12.5
site: Chang’an · 34.27, 108.9
site: Palmyra · 34.55, 38.27
site: Muziris · 10.2, 76.2
area: Taklamakan · 39, 83
area: Indian Ocean · -5, 75

Silk passed west through Central Asian intermediaries; Roman gold, silver and manufactured goods travelled east. The **Parthian and Kushan worlds** linked these exchanges with India and Han China.

Roads and rivers fed regional markets. Ships joined Roman Egypt to Indian ports through the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, with **Aksum**’s port of Adulis on the way. Baltic amber came south along the **Amber Road** to Aquileia and Rome. **Ctesiphon**, rather than the later city of Baghdad, anchors Mesopotamia here.

- silk: **Silk** · China → west and south
- gold-silver: **Gold & silver** · Roman world → east
- glass-metals: **Glass, copper & tin** · Mediterranean → India
- horses: **Horses** · Fergana → China
- spices-cotton: **Spices & cotton** · India & Aksum → Roman world
- lapis-amber: **Amber** · Baltic → Rome

> Selected corridors around 150 CE, not imperial borders or single journeys. Random dots show direction; their frequency does not represent volume. Constantinople and the Sui–Tang canal network belong to later periods.

## americas-exchange
### Classic Mesoamerica and Hopewell
spot: 19.7, -98.85
view: fit
site: Teotihuacan · 19.69, -98.84
site: Nazca · -14.83, -74.94
area: Mesoamerica · 17, -92
area: Andes · -15, -72

Around 400 CE, **Teotihuacan** controlled the Pachuca obsidian trade and reached deep into the Maya world, while Maya jade and cacao moved the other way. In the Ohio valley, **Hopewell** communities gathered obsidian from Yellowstone, copper from Lake Superior and shell from the Gulf.

In the Caribbean, **Saladoid** pottery makers had spread from the Orinoco through the Lesser Antilles to Puerto Rico. Spondylus continued to reach the Moche coast.

- obsidian: **Obsidian** · Pachuca & El Chayal → cities; Yellowstone → Ohio
- jade: **Jade** · Motagua → Maya cities and Teotihuacan
- shell: **Spondylus & shell** · Gulf → Ohio; Ecuador → Peru
- metals: **Copper & metals** · Lake Superior → Ohio
- crops: **Crops** · Soconusco cacao → Teotihuacan
- ceramics: **Pottery & river networks** · Saladoid islands; Amazon, Rio Negro and Orinoco

> Sourcing studies identify origins; the corridors between them are schematic. Amazonian river links are drawn fainter.

## african-networks
### Garamantes and Aksum
spot: 14.1, 38.7
view: fit
site: Aksum · 14.13, 38.72
site: Meroë · 16.94, 33.72
site: Carthage · 36.85, 10.32
area: Sahara · 22, 10
area: Red Sea · 20, 38

Around 200 CE the **Garamantes** of the Fezzan linked the Roman coast with the Sahara, and probably with the Niger bend, trading salt, carnelian and captives. On the Nile, **Meroë** sent gold, ivory and iron north to Roman Egypt, and Egyptian and Roman goods came upriver.

In the Horn, **Aksum** exported ivory through its port at Adulis and traded across the Red Sea with South Arabia.

- gold-ivory: **Gold, ivory & ebony** · Meroë and Aksum → Egypt and the Red Sea
- salt-copper: **Salt & copper** · Sahara → coast and Sahel
- cloth-beads: **Cloth, beads & wine** · Roman world → Africa
- captives: **Enslaved people** · Sahara and Nile → the Mediterranean

> Garamantian routes south of the Fezzan are inferred from graves, wells and imports, so they are drawn fainter. Bantu-speaking expansions in the same centuries are on the human migrations story.
